description: This topic examines the chemical nature and composition of soil, soil formation by weathering, soil texture and pH, plant nutrients, fertilisers, cation exchange and the conservation of soil chemistry using Tanzanian agricultural examples.

mcq.questionText: Which of the following is NOT one of the main components of a typical fertile soil?
mcq.explanation: A fertile soil is made up of mineral particles, humus (organic matter), water, air and living organisms. Liquefied petroleum gas is a fuel and is not a natural component of soil.

mcq.questionText: The breaking down of rocks into smaller particles to form soil is called:
mcq.explanation: Weathering is the gradual breakdown of rocks into smaller mineral particles through physical, chemical and biological processes, and it is the first stage of soil formation.

mcq.questionText: Which type of weathering involves a chemical reaction such as the action of acidic rain on rocks?
mcq.explanation: Chemical weathering changes the chemical composition of rock minerals, for example when weak carbonic acid in rainwater reacts with limestone (calcium carbonate) and dissolves it.

mcq.questionText: A soil that contains a balanced mixture of sand, silt, clay and humus, and is considered the best for most crops, is called:
mcq.explanation: Loam soil is a balanced mixture of sand, silt, clay and humus. It drains well yet retains enough water and nutrients, making it the most suitable soil for most crops such as maize and beans.

mcq.questionText: Which property best describes sandy soil?

options.text: Holds water strongly and drains slowly
Large particles, drains quickly and holds little water
Very small particles that become sticky when wet

mcq.explanation: Sandy soil has large particles with wide spaces between them, so it allows water to drain through quickly and retains little water and few dissolved nutrients.

mcq.questionText: A soil sample tested with universal indicator gives a pH of 5. The soil is:
mcq.explanation: A pH below 7 indicates acidity. A pH of 5 means the soil is acidic; pH 7 would be neutral and a pH above 7 would be alkaline.

mcq.questionText: Which substance is commonly added to neutralise an acidic soil (liming)?
mcq.explanation: Liming uses calcium-containing bases such as quicklime (CaO), slaked lime (Ca(OH)2) or limestone (CaCO3). These bases neutralise excess acidity and raise the soil pH towards neutral.

mcq.questionText: The three main (macro) nutrient elements most often supplied to crops by fertilisers are:
mcq.explanation: Nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P) and potassium (K) are the three primary macronutrients that plants need in large amounts and that are commonly contained in fertilisers such as NPK.

mcq.questionText: Which of the following is an example of organic manure rather than an artificial fertiliser?
mcq.explanation: Organic manure is derived from plant or animal matter, such as cattle dung, compost and green manure. Urea, ammonium sulphate and NPK are manufactured inorganic (artificial) fertilisers.

mcq.questionText: Nitrogen is most important to plants because it is needed for the formation of:
mcq.explanation: Nitrogen is a key element in proteins, chlorophyll and many enzymes. A nitrogen deficiency causes yellowing of leaves and stunted growth, so nitrogen fertilisers promote healthy green leafy growth.

mcq.questionText: Cation exchange in soil refers to the ability of soil particles to:

options.text: Release oxygen gas to plant roots
Hold and exchange positively charged nutrient ions such as K+, Ca2+ and Mg2+
Destroy all living organisms in the soil

mcq.explanation: Clay and humus carry negative charges that attract and hold positively charged ions (cations) such as K+, Ca2+, Mg2+ and NH4+. These cations can be exchanged and taken up by plant roots, which is the basis of soil fertility.

mcq.questionText: Which soil type has the highest capacity to hold water and nutrients but drains poorly and becomes sticky when wet?
mcq.explanation: Clay soil has very small particles with tiny spaces between them, so it holds a lot of water and nutrients but drains poorly, becomes waterlogged easily and turns sticky when wet and hard when dry.

mcq.questionText: Humus improves soil fertility mainly because it:

options.text: Increases soil acidity to harmful levels
Supplies nutrients and improves water retention and structure
Removes all air from the soil

mcq.explanation: Humus is decomposed organic matter. It slowly releases nutrients, improves the ability of soil to hold water, increases cation exchange capacity and improves soil structure and aeration.

mcq.questionText: Continuous use of certain ammonium-based nitrogen fertilisers over many seasons tends to make the soil:
mcq.explanation: Ammonium ions from fertilisers such as ammonium sulphate are converted by soil bacteria into nitrate, releasing hydrogen ions (H+) that lower the pH. This is why long-term use of these fertilisers acidifies the soil and may require liming.

mcq.questionText: Which practice helps to conserve soil and protect its chemistry from degradation?

options.text: Burning all crop residues every season
Crop rotation and adding organic manure
Removing all vegetation cover from slopes

mcq.explanation: Crop rotation, adding organic manure, planting cover crops and contour ploughing all maintain nutrient balance, reduce erosion and conserve soil structure and chemistry, unlike burning residues or continuous monocropping.

fib.questionText: The decomposed organic matter in soil that improves its fertility is called _____.
fib.explanation: Humus is dark, decomposed organic matter formed from dead plants and animals. It supplies nutrients and improves water retention and soil structure.

fib.questionText: The process by which rocks are broken down to form soil is known as _____.
fib.explanation: Weathering breaks rocks into smaller particles through physical, chemical and biological action, and it is the starting point of soil formation.

fib.questionText: A soil with a pH of exactly 7 is described as _____.
fib.explanation: A pH of 7 indicates a neutral soil, meaning it is neither acidic (below 7) nor alkaline (above 7).

fib.questionText: The addition of lime to reduce the acidity of soil is called _____.
fib.explanation: Liming is the application of calcium bases such as quicklime, slaked lime or limestone to neutralise excess acid and raise the soil pH.

fib.questionText: The chemical symbol for the macronutrient potassium is _____.
fib.explanation: Potassium is represented by the symbol K (from the Latin name kalium). It is one of the three primary plant macronutrients, N, P and K.

fib.questionText: Soil that is made up of large particles, drains quickly and holds little water is called _____ soil.
fib.explanation: Sandy soil has large particles with wide air spaces, so water and dissolved nutrients drain away quickly.

fib.questionText: Negatively charged clay and humus particles attract and hold positively charged ions in a process called _____ exchange.
fib.explanation: Cation exchange is the holding and swapping of positive ions (cations) such as K+, Ca2+ and NH4+ by negatively charged clay and humus, which allows plant roots to take up nutrients.

fib.questionText: The instrument or paper commonly used to measure the pH of a soil sample is called a/an _____.
fib.explanation: Universal indicator (or a pH meter) is used to measure soil pH. A soil suspension is mixed with the indicator and the colour produced is compared with a pH colour chart.

fib.questionText: Fertilisers obtained from plant and animal remains, such as compost and farmyard manure, are called _____ manure.
fib.explanation: Organic manure comes from decomposed plant and animal matter. It releases nutrients slowly and improves soil structure, unlike manufactured inorganic fertilisers.

fib.questionText: The nutrient element nitrogen is mainly responsible for the green colour of leaves because it is part of the pigment _____.
fib.explanation: Nitrogen is a component of chlorophyll, the green pigment used in photosynthesis. A shortage of nitrogen causes leaves to turn yellow (chlorosis).

tf.questionText: Soil is made up only of mineral particles and contains no air or water.
tf.explanation: Soil contains mineral particles, humus, water, air and living organisms. The spaces between particles hold both air and water, which are essential for plant roots and soil organisms.

tf.questionText: Physical weathering breaks rocks into smaller pieces without changing their chemical composition.
tf.explanation: Physical (mechanical) weathering, for example by temperature changes that cause rocks to expand and crack, breaks rocks into smaller particles but does not change their chemical make-up.

tf.questionText: A soil with a pH of 9 is alkaline.
tf.explanation: Any pH above 7 indicates an alkaline soil. A pH of 9 is clearly above neutral, so the soil is alkaline.

tf.questionText: Adding lime to a soil lowers its pH and makes it more acidic.
tf.explanation: Lime is a base, so it neutralises acid and raises the pH towards neutral or alkaline. It does not lower the pH or increase acidity.

tf.questionText: Clay soil holds more water and nutrients than sandy soil.
tf.explanation: Clay has very small particles with tiny spaces, giving it a large surface area that holds more water and more nutrient ions than coarse, large-particled sandy soil.

tf.questionText: Nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium are all plant macronutrients.
tf.explanation: Nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P) and potassium (K) are the three primary macronutrients that plants require in relatively large quantities for healthy growth.

tf.questionText: Organic manure releases its nutrients more slowly than most artificial inorganic fertilisers.
tf.explanation: Organic manure must first decompose before its nutrients become available, so it releases nutrients slowly. Inorganic fertilisers are usually soluble and act more quickly.

tf.questionText: Humus increases the cation exchange capacity of a soil.
tf.explanation: Humus carries negative charges that attract and hold positively charged nutrient ions, so adding humus increases the soil's cation exchange capacity and its ability to supply nutrients.

tf.questionText: Soil erosion has no effect on the chemical fertility of soil.
tf.explanation: Erosion removes the fertile topsoil that is rich in humus and nutrients, reducing soil fertility. It is a major form of soil degradation that must be controlled by conservation methods.

tf.questionText: Living organisms such as earthworms and bacteria play no role in soil formation or fertility.
tf.explanation: Living organisms aid biological weathering, decompose organic matter into humus, aerate the soil and recycle nutrients, so they are very important for both soil formation and fertility.

summary.questionText: List the five main components of a fertile soil.
summary.correctAnswer: The five main components of a fertile soil are mineral particles, humus (organic matter), water, air and living organisms.
summary.explanation: A balanced soil contains weathered mineral particles, decomposed organic matter (humus), water and air held in the pore spaces, and living organisms such as bacteria, fungi and earthworms.

summary.questionText: Briefly explain the three types of weathering involved in soil formation.
summary.correctAnswer: Physical weathering breaks rocks into smaller pieces without changing their chemistry (e.g. heating and cooling). Chemical weathering changes the chemical composition of rock minerals (e.g. acid rain dissolving limestone). Biological weathering is caused by living things, such as plant roots splitting rocks and organisms releasing acids.
summary.explanation: Soil forms through a combination of physical, chemical and biological weathering acting on parent rock over long periods.

summary.questionText: Compare the properties of sandy soil and clay soil.
summary.correctAnswer: Sandy soil has large particles, drains quickly, is well aerated but holds little water and few nutrients. Clay soil has very small particles, drains slowly, holds a lot of water and nutrients, becomes sticky when wet and hard when dry, and can become waterlogged.
summary.explanation: Particle size controls drainage, aeration and the ability to hold water and nutrients, which is why sandy and clay soils behave very differently.

summary.questionText: Describe how to test the pH of a soil sample in the laboratory.
summary.correctAnswer: Mix a small amount of soil with distilled water and shake, then allow it to settle. Add a few drops of universal indicator to the soil suspension (or use a pH meter or indicator paper) and compare the colour produced with a pH colour chart to read the pH value.
summary.explanation: Soil pH is found by making a soil-water suspension and measuring its pH with universal indicator, indicator paper or a pH meter.

summary.questionText: Explain how an acidic soil can be corrected.
summary.correctAnswer: An acidic soil is corrected by adding a base such as quicklime (CaO), slaked lime (Ca(OH)2) or limestone (CaCO3). The base neutralises the excess acid, raising the pH towards neutral and improving conditions for crop growth.
summary.explanation: Liming with calcium-containing bases is the standard method of neutralising soil acidity and raising pH.

summary.questionText: State the roles of nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium in plant growth.
summary.correctAnswer: Nitrogen promotes healthy green leafy growth and is needed for proteins and chlorophyll. Phosphorus supports root development, flowering and seed formation. Potassium strengthens plants, helps disease resistance and supports fruit and grain formation.
summary.explanation: N, P and K are the three primary macronutrients, each with distinct functions in healthy plant growth and yield.

summary.questionText: Compare organic manure and inorganic (artificial) fertilisers.
summary.correctAnswer: Organic manure comes from plant and animal matter, releases nutrients slowly, improves soil structure and adds humus, but contains lower concentrations of nutrients. Inorganic fertilisers are manufactured, contain high concentrations of specific nutrients and act quickly, but do not improve soil structure and may acidify the soil with continued use.
summary.explanation: Both supply nutrients, but they differ in source, speed of action, nutrient concentration and effect on soil structure and pH.

summary.questionText: Explain the meaning of cation exchange in soil and why it is important.
summary.correctAnswer: Cation exchange is the ability of negatively charged clay and humus particles to attract, hold and release positively charged nutrient ions such as K+, Ca2+, Mg2+ and NH4+. It is important because it stores nutrients in the soil and allows plant roots to take them up gradually instead of losing them to leaching.
summary.explanation: Cation exchange capacity is a key measure of how well a soil can retain and supply nutrient cations to plants.

summary.questionText: Outline the main causes of soil degradation that affect soil chemistry.
summary.correctAnswer: Soil degradation is caused by soil erosion (loss of fertile topsoil), leaching of nutrients, overuse of acidifying fertilisers, continuous monocropping without rest, burning of crop residues and loss of organic matter and vegetation cover.
summary.explanation: These processes remove or lock up nutrients, change soil pH and reduce humus, lowering the chemical fertility of the soil.

summary.questionText: Suggest ways of conserving the chemical fertility of soil.
summary.correctAnswer: Soil fertility can be conserved by adding organic manure and compost, practising crop rotation, planting leguminous (cover) crops to fix nitrogen, controlling erosion with contour ploughing and terraces, liming acidic soils and avoiding the burning of crop residues.
summary.explanation: These conservation practices maintain humus, nutrient balance and a suitable pH while reducing nutrient loss and erosion.

hoq.questionText: A maize farmer in the Southern Highlands of Tanzania finds his soil has a pH of 4.5 and crops grow poorly. He adds 200 kg of slaked lime, Ca(OH)2, per hectare. Which statement best explains the chemistry of what happens to the soil after liming?

options.text: The Ca(OH)2 releases hydroxide ions that neutralise excess H+ ions, raising the pH towards neutral and improving nutrient availability
The Ca(OH)2 adds more H+ ions, lowering the pH further and harming the crop
The Ca(OH)2 turns the soil into pure clay so no nutrients can be held
The Ca(OH)2 evaporates immediately and has no effect on soil pH

hoq.explanation: Slaked lime is a base. Its hydroxide ions (OH-) react with and neutralise the excess hydrogen ions (H+) responsible for acidity, raising the soil pH from 4.5 towards neutral. At a more favourable pH, nutrients such as phosphorus become more available, improving crop growth.

hoq.questionText: Two soil samples are tested. Sample X drains very quickly and dries within minutes after watering, while Sample Y becomes waterlogged and sticky and holds water for days. A farmer wants to improve both for growing vegetables. What is the best single amendment to add to BOTH samples, and why?

options.text: Add sand to both, because sand always increases fertility
Add humus/organic matter to both, because it improves water retention in sandy soil and improves drainage and structure in clay soil
Add concentrated acid to both, to dissolve the particles
Add common salt to both, to hold the nutrients in place

hoq.explanation: Sample X behaves like sandy soil and Sample Y like clay. Adding humus (organic matter) benefits both: in sandy soil it increases water and nutrient retention, while in clay soil it opens up the structure to improve drainage and aeration. It also raises the cation exchange capacity, improving fertility.

hoq.questionText: A farmer applies large amounts of ammonium sulphate, (NH4)2SO4, to his field every season for several years. He notices the soil becomes increasingly acidic and yields fall. Which explanation and remedy is correct?

options.text: Soil bacteria convert NH4+ to nitrate, releasing H+ ions that lower the pH; the remedy is to apply lime to neutralise the acidity
The sulphate ions are basic, so the soil becomes alkaline; the remedy is to add more ammonium sulphate
The fertiliser removes all water from the soil; the remedy is to stop irrigating
The fertiliser adds humus too fast; the remedy is to burn the topsoil

hoq.explanation: When ammonium ions (NH4+) are nitrified by soil bacteria into nitrate (NO3-), hydrogen ions (H+) are released, which lowers the soil pH over time. The acidity reduces nutrient availability and yields. Applying lime neutralises the excess acid and restores a suitable pH; rotating with organic manure also helps.
